title: Multiplication as Equal Groups
subject: Math
developmentNotes: Third graders are moving from repeated addition into multiplicative reasoning. Keep models concrete and visual before asking for equations.
learningObjective: Students will explain multiplication as equal groups, represent multiplication with repeated addition and arrays, and solve one-step equal-group word problems.
essentialQuestion: What does multiplication really mean before we calculate it?

vocabularyTerms.definition: groups that each have the same amount
the answer to a multiplication problem
objects arranged in equal rows and columns
adding the same number again and again

prerequisites: Recognize rows, columns, and groups of objects

hook.content: A garden has 4 baskets. Each basket has 5 apples. The gardener writes 4 × 5. Students predict what each number means before finding the total.
hook.studentAction: Predict, notice, or explain initial thinking before direct instruction.
hook.teacherOrAppAction: Capture initial response as non-graded diagnostic evidence.

miniTeach.content: Multiplication is a way to count equal groups efficiently. In 4 × 5, there are 4 groups and each group has 5. That can be written as 5 + 5 + 5 + 5, drawn as 4 rows of 5, or solved as 20.
miniTeach.cognitiveLoadNotes: Use short chunks, one example at a time, and reveal labels only after students observe the model.

known: All baskets have the same number of apples.
rules: Equal groups can be counted with repeated addition.
A multiplication expression can represent repeated equal groups.
If the groups are not equal, multiplication does not directly fit until the groups are adjusted or described differently.
avoid: Do not add the two factors once, such as 4 + 5.
Do not multiply when groups are unequal without explaining the change.
steps: Name the amount in each group.
Solve and check by skip-counting or drawing.
firstPrinciplesBreakdown.check: Skip-count by the amount in each group: 5, 10, 15, 20.

workedExample.content: Problem: 3 boxes have 6 crayons in each box. Known facts: 3 boxes, 6 crayons each. Repeated addition: 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. Multiplication: 3 × 6 = 18. Answer: 18 crayons.
workedExample.teacherOrAppAction: Highlight each reasoning step and connect it to the first-principles breakdown.

items: Draw 2 groups of 4 stars. Write the repeated addition and multiplication expression.
Match 5 + 5 + 5 to 3 × 5. Explain why it is not 5 × 3 in this story model.
Use an array to show 4 × 3 and label rows and columns.
Debug this model: 3 groups are shown as 4, 4, and 5. Can it be represented by one multiplication fact? Why or why not?
guidedPractice.scaffolding: Start with high support, then remove hints. Require explanation on the final item.

criticalThinkingCheckpoint.prompt: A student says 4 × 5 means 4 + 5. What is the mistake? Explain how equal groups help fix the reasoning.
criticalThinkingCheckpoint.lookFor: Student identifies assumption, evaluates reasoning, and explains why one answer or model is stronger.

evidenceBasedReasoningTask.prompt: Claim: 3 × 4 = 12. Prove the claim using at least two kinds of evidence: repeated addition, an array, or a word story.

interpretationOrDiscussionTask.prompt: An array with 2 rows and 6 columns can be read as 2 groups of 6 or 6 columns of 2. Discuss what changes and what stays the same.
interpretationOrDiscussionTask.safety: Use private response or moderated classroom mode only. No unrestricted student chat.

activePractice.content: Students drag objects into equal baskets. The app highlights unequal groups and asks students to debug the model before writing the equation.

reteachPath.misconception: Student adds the two factors instead of forming equal groups.
reteachPath.simpleExplanation: Multiplication asks two questions: how many groups, and how many in each group?
steps: Write the same addend once for each group.
Check with a drawing or array.
reteachPath.exitCriteria: Student completes at least 4 of 5 reteach items and explains the corrected misconception.

tasks: Create two different arrays that both show 12. Explain why both work.
Write a word problem for 6 × 4 and solve it using repeated addition, an array, and multiplication.
Compare 3 × 4 and 4 × 3. Explain what changes in the story and what stays the same.
challengePath.extensionRule: Unlock at 90+ mastery or teacher/parent assignment; still schedule Memory Vault review.

successCriteria: I can build equal groups with objects or drawings.
I can connect equal groups, repeated addition, and an array.
I can write a multiplication equation that matches my model.
I can explain what each factor and the product mean.

knowledge: An array can show rows, columns, and a total.
capability: Build, draw, and label an equal-group model.
reasoning: Check whether an equation matches the groups instead of guessing from the numbers.
retention: Recall the meaning of factors and product after a delay.
transfer: Use multiplication to describe a new classroom, toy, or snack grouping.

phaseModules.title: Meet the group builder
phaseModules.studentAction: Make equal groups with counters and predict how many objects there will be altogether.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can tell what is equal about the groups.

phaseModules.title: See groups become an equation
phaseModules.studentAction: Watch objects become a drawing, repeated addition, an array, and a multiplication equation.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can match each equation number to the model.

phaseModules.title: Name the parts
phaseModules.studentAction: Point to the groups, group size, number of groups, factors, and product in a model.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can explain what each part means.

phaseModules.title: Build and draw
phaseModules.studentAction: Create several equal-group models, then write the repeated addition and multiplication sentence.
phaseModules.successCheck: The drawing, addition, and equation show the same total.

phaseModules.title: Show what you know
phaseModules.studentAction: Solve a new equal-group story and explain your model with words or a picture.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can prove the answer with a matching model.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve the group rule
phaseModules.studentAction: Return later and explain what multiplication means without seeing the counters.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can recall equal groups and product meaning.

phaseModules.title: Use groups in a new place
phaseModules.studentAction: Find or invent equal groups in a classroom, game, snack, or toy situation.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can use the idea when the objects change.

phaseModules.title: Choose the next move
phaseModules.studentAction: If the groups are unequal, fix them; if the model is secure, create a story for a partner.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can choose a helpful repair or challenge.

proofTasks.prompt: Explain how an array shows equal groups.
Solve a new equal-group story with a model and equation.

Create a multiplication story from a new group situation.

feedbackRules.result: The learner counts groups that do not have the same amount.
feedbackRules.hint: Check each group before writing the equation.

feedbackRules.result: The learner swaps the group information and total.
feedbackRules.hint: Say how many groups, how many in each, and how many altogether.

feedbackRules.result: The equation does not match the drawing.
feedbackRules.hint: Point to each number in the picture before rewriting.
feedbackRules.action: Connect objects, addition, and equation again.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner cannot build equal groups.
reteachPaths.action: Use three small groups of counters and have the learner check each group aloud before drawing.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot count each group reliably.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Practice one-to-one counting and grouping by twos or fives before writing multiplication.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner explains a model independently.
challengePaths.action: Create two different stories for the same multiplication equation and compare them.

parentTeacherNotes: Ask the student to make equal groups with coins, snacks, or toys. Require them to explain the groups before giving the answer.
accessibilityNotes: Use plain, grade-appropriate language and define academic vocabulary before using it in prompts.
Provide alt text or text-equivalent descriptions for every image, diagram, array, chart, map, or model.
Make all interactive elements keyboard accessible with visible focus states and screen-reader labels.
Never rely only on color to communicate correct/incorrect, categories, or importance.
Provide read-aloud support for Foundation Academy and optional read-aloud for all grade bands.
Chunk instructions into short steps and provide examples before independent work.
safetyNotes: No public student posting, random direct messages, or unrestricted discussion.
Discussion prompts must use sentence frames and moderation/teacher controls when implemented.
Student-generated work should be visible only to the student and authorized parent/teacher roles unless explicitly assigned in a safe classroom workflow.
Do not collect unnecessary personal information in lesson responses.
implementationNotes: Render lessonFlow sections in order with progress state.
Persist quiz attempts and item-level skill tags.
Generate Memory Vault records after lesson completion.
Use mastery bands to branch to reteach, guided practice, review, or challenge.
Store open responses privately with role-based access.
Use answer keys and rubrics for review; do not expose hidden answer keys in student mode.
